notes.b: Acids show a common set of properties that can be observed in the laboratory and at home. These shared properties are how we decide whether a substance counts as an acid.
points: Acids taste sour, but laboratory chemicals must never be tasted because many are corrosive or poisonous.
Acids turn blue litmus (a dye that changes colour in acids and bases) red, and they have a pH below 7 (pH is a number that describes how acidic or basic a solution is).
Acids react with reactive metals such as magnesium and zinc to give hydrogen gas, so bubbles form on the metal.
Acids react with carbonates (compounds containing the CO₃²⁻ ion, such as chalk) to give carbon dioxide, seen as fizzing.
Acids neutralise bases, which means they react with them so that both lose their acidic or basic character.
Examples: hydrochloric acid (HCl), sulfuric acid (H₂SO₄), nitric acid (HNO₃), ethanoic acid (CH₃COOH, in vinegar) and citric acid (in citrus fruits).
notes.tip: If asked for properties of acids, give several: sour taste, blue litmus turns red, pH below 7, reaction with metals and carbonates, and neutralising bases.

notes.b: Bases are the chemical opposites of acids. Their properties mirror those of acids, and some of them dissolve in water to form alkalis.
points: Bases taste bitter and feel soapy or slippery, because they react with the oils on the skin.
Bases turn red litmus blue and have a pH above 7.
Bases neutralise acids, so an acid and a base each cancel out the other's properties.
An alkali is a base that dissolves in water, e.g. sodium hydroxide (NaOH), potassium hydroxide (KOH) and aqueous ammonia (NH₃), which is ammonia dissolved in water.
Many bases are insoluble in water, e.g. copper(II) oxide and magnesium hydroxide, so they are not alkalis.

Concentrated alkalis (those with a lot of dissolved base in a small volume of water) are corrosive, meaning they damage skin and other materials: sodium hydroxide is the main ingredient of oven cleaners and drain cleaners.
notes.tip: Not all bases are alkalis: an alkali is a soluble base. Don't call copper(II) oxide or magnesium hydroxide an alkali.

notes.b: You cannot tell whether a clear solution is acidic or basic by looking at it, so chemists add an indicator. An indicator is a substance that changes colour depending on whether it is in an acidic or a basic solution.
points: Litmus is red in acid and blue in base, so it is the simplest test for which kind of solution you have.
Phenolphthalein is colourless in acid and pink in base; it changes colour between pH 8.3 and pH 10.
Methyl orange is red in acid and yellow in base; it changes colour between pH 3.1 and pH 4.4.
Universal indicator is a mixture of indicators, so it gives a range of colours across the pH scale: red in strong acid, through orange, yellow and green at pH 7, to blue and purple in strong base.
Natural indicators, such as red cabbage extract, also change colour between acidic and basic solutions.
notes.tip: Exams ask you to name an indicator and give its colours in acid and in base, so learn both colours for litmus, phenolphthalein and methyl orange.

notes.b: Common substances are classed as acids or bases according to the properties they show. For each one, the category is justified by a property you can observe or a substance it contains.
points: Vinegar is an acid: it contains ethanoic acid, tastes sour, turns blue litmus red and fizzes with baking soda.
Citric juices are acids: lemon juice contains citric acid, tastes sour and has a pH of about 2–3; orange juice has a pH of about 3–4.
Antacids (medicines for excess stomach acid) are bases: they contain magnesium hydroxide, aluminium hydroxide, calcium carbonate or sodium hydrogencarbonate, and neutralise excess stomach acid.
Toothpaste is mildly basic, so it neutralises the acids that bacteria in plaque (the film of bacteria on teeth) produce, which would otherwise attack tooth enamel (the hard outer layer of the tooth).
Baking soda (sodium hydrogencarbonate) is a weak base.
Oven cleaner (sodium hydroxide) is a strong alkali, which is why it is corrosive and must be handled with care.
Lemonade and cola are acids because they contain citric, carbonic or phosphoric acid.
notes.tip: Exams ask you to justify a category using properties. For vinegar use sour taste, litmus turning red and fizzing with carbonates; for antacids use pH above 7, litmus turning blue and neutralising acid.

notes.b: Neutralisation is the reaction of an acid with a base to form a salt and water; the acid and base cancel out each other's properties. This is useful whenever something is too acidic and needs to be corrected.
points: Lime in agriculture: crops grow poorly in acidic soil, so farmers spread lime (calcium oxide or calcium hydroxide) or ground limestone (calcium carbonate) to neutralise the acid and raise the soil pH.
Ground limestone in soil: CaCO₃ + 2H⁺ → Ca²⁺ + H₂O + CO₂. Here H⁺ stands for the acid in the soil.
Acid indigestion: the stomach contains hydrochloric acid, and excess acid causes indigestion and heartburn, so a base is taken to remove it.
Antacid tablets neutralise the excess acid, e.g. Mg(OH)₂ + 2HCl → MgCl₂ + 2H₂O.
Sodium hydrogencarbonate in an antacid also neutralises stomach acid: NaHCO₃ + HCl → NaCl + H₂O + CO₂.
Lime is added to acidic lakes to neutralise the acid, so the water becomes less acidic.
Toothpaste neutralises plaque acid, and baking soda is a claimed remedy for a bee sting, which is said to be acidic.
notes.tip: Exams ask for everyday examples of neutralisation, such as antacids and lime in agriculture, with equations. Learn one balanced equation for each.

notes.b: Acid–base reactions produce salts, and the name of a salt comes from the acid and the metal. Knowing this lets you name the product of any acid reaction.
points: A salt is a compound formed when the hydrogen of an acid is replaced by a metal ion or an ammonium ion (NH₄⁺).
Hydrochloric acid gives chlorides, e.g. NaCl, because the chloride ion Cl⁻ is what remains of the acid.
Sulfuric acid gives sulfates; nitric acid gives nitrates; ethanoic acid gives ethanoates; carbonic acid gives carbonates.
Sulfuric acid is diprotic, with two replaceable hydrogens, so one mole of it (a fixed amount of substance) reacts with twice as much sodium hydroxide as one mole of hydrochloric acid does.
notes.tip: You may be asked to name the salt formed: take the metal's name, then the ending given by the acid.

notes.b: General word equation: acid + base → salt + water. A base here includes metal oxides and hydroxides, and ammonia.
points: HCl(aq) + NaOH(aq) → NaCl(aq) + H₂O(l)
H₂SO₄(aq) + 2KOH(aq) → K₂SO₄(aq) + 2H₂O(l)
With an insoluble metal oxide: 2HCl(aq) + CuO(s) → CuCl₂(aq) + H₂O(l); the black solid dissolves to give a blue solution.
With ammonia: NH₃(aq) + HCl(aq) → NH₄Cl(aq); this forms an ammonium salt and no water.
Ionic equation (showing only the ions that react) for any strong acid and strong alkali: H⁺(aq) + OH⁻(aq) → H₂O(l).
Neutralisation is exothermic, so it releases heat.
notes.tip: Exams ask you to complete and balance equations for acids with bases, and to name the salt formed.

notes.b: General word equation: acid + metal → salt + hydrogen. This applies to metals above hydrogen in reactivity, such as magnesium, zinc and iron.
points: Mg(s) + 2HCl(aq) → MgCl₂(aq) + H₂(g): the magnesium disappears, the mixture fizzes and the flask gets warm.
Zn(s) + H₂SO₄(aq) → ZnSO₄(aq) + H₂(g).
Copper does not react with dilute hydrochloric or sulfuric acid, because it is below hydrogen in the electrochemical series (the list of metals in order of reactivity).
Test for hydrogen: a lighted splint held at the mouth of the tube gives a squeaky pop.
notes.tip: Metal + acid gives hydrogen, not water. Don't confuse the splint test for hydrogen with the limewater test for carbon dioxide. You may be asked to name the gas and describe its test.

notes.b: General word equation: acid + carbonate → salt + water + carbon dioxide. Hydrogencarbonates (compounds containing the HCO₃⁻ ion) behave the same way.
points: CaCO₃(s) + 2HCl(aq) → CaCl₂(aq) + H₂O(l) + CO₂(g); acids react with carbonates even when the carbonate is insoluble, as calcium carbonate is.
Na₂CO₃(aq) + H₂SO₄(aq) → Na₂SO₄(aq) + H₂O(l) + CO₂(g).
Hydrogencarbonates react the same way: NaHCO₃(s) + HCl(aq) → NaCl(aq) + H₂O(l) + CO₂(g).
Test for carbon dioxide: it turns limewater (a solution of calcium hydroxide) milky, Ca(OH)₂(aq) + CO₂(g) → CaCO₃(s) + H₂O(l).
notes.tip: Acids react with carbonates even if the carbonate is insoluble, such as CaCO₃. Use limewater for CO₂ and the lighted splint for H₂, and don't mix them up.

notes.b: Use this method to write the equation for any reaction of an acid. It works because each type of reaction always gives the same pattern of products.
points: Step 1: Identify the reaction type from the other reactant: a base, a metal, or a carbonate or hydrogencarbonate.
Step 2: Name the salt from the metal (or ammonium) ion and the acid.
Step 3: Add the other products: water for a base; hydrogen for a metal; water and carbon dioxide for a carbonate or hydrogencarbonate.
Step 4: Balance the equation, so that each element has the same number of atoms on both sides.
Example: magnesium oxide and nitric acid give MgO(s) + 2HNO₃(aq) → Mg(NO₃)₂(aq) + H₂O(l), magnesium nitrate.
Example: potassium carbonate and ethanoic acid give K₂CO₃ + 2CH₃COOH → 2CH₃COOK + H₂O + CO₂, potassium ethanoate.
notes.tip: Exams ask you to write balanced equations for an acid with a metal, a carbonate and a base, name the salt, and describe a test for the gas. Work through the four steps in order.

keyTerms.definition: A substance with a pH below 7 that tastes sour, turns blue litmus red and neutralises bases.
A substance with a pH above 7 that turns red litmus blue, tastes bitter and neutralises acids.
A base that dissolves in water.
A substance that changes colour depending on whether it is in an acidic or a basic solution.
A mixture of indicators that gives a range of colours across the pH scale.
The reaction of an acid with a base to form a salt and water, in which the acid and base cancel out each other's properties.
A base that neutralises excess stomach acid, e.g. magnesium hydroxide.
Able to destroy or burn skin and other materials, as concentrated acids and alkalis are.
A compound formed when the hydrogen of an acid is replaced by a metal ion or an ammonium ion.
An acid with two replaceable hydrogen atoms, such as sulfuric acid.
A salt containing the ammonium ion, NH₄⁺, such as ammonium chloride, formed when ammonia reacts with an acid.
An equation showing only the ions and molecules that take part in the change, e.g. H⁺(aq) + OH⁻(aq) → H₂O(l).
Describes a reaction that releases heat to the surroundings.
A test for carbon dioxide: the gas turns limewater milky.
A test for hydrogen: a lighted splint held at the mouth of the tube gives a squeaky pop.

questions.prompt: Using two properties of each, explain why vinegar is classed as an acid and antacid tablets are classed as bases.
questions.model: Vinegar is an acid because it contains ethanoic acid, which turns blue litmus red, showing a pH below 7. Vinegar also reacts with carbonates: it fizzes with baking soda, giving off carbon dioxide. Antacid tablets are bases because they contain magnesium hydroxide, aluminium hydroxide, calcium carbonate or sodium hydrogencarbonate, which turn red litmus blue, showing a pH above 7. Antacids also neutralise acids: they neutralise excess stomach acid.

questions.prompt: Describe two everyday examples of neutralisation, and write a balanced equation for one of them.
questions.model: Example 1: farmers spread lime (calcium oxide or calcium hydroxide) or ground limestone (calcium carbonate) on acidic soil. The base neutralises the acid, raising the soil pH, so crops grow better. Example 2: antacid tablets neutralise excess hydrochloric acid in the stomach, relieving acid indigestion and heartburn. Balanced equation for the antacid: Mg(OH)₂ + 2HCl → MgCl₂ + 2H₂O.

questions.prompt: Write balanced equations for the reactions of hydrochloric acid with (i) zinc, (ii) sodium carbonate, (iii) calcium hydroxide.
questions.model: (i) Zn + 2HCl → ZnCl₂ + H₂. (ii) Na₂CO₃ + 2HCl → 2NaCl + H₂O + CO₂. (iii) Ca(OH)₂ + 2HCl → CaCl₂ + 2H₂O.

questions.prompt: Name the gas produced when magnesium reacts with dilute sulfuric acid, write the balanced equation, and describe a test for the gas.
questions.model: The gas is hydrogen. Mg + H₂SO₄ → MgSO₄ + H₂. Test: a lighted splint held at the mouth of the tube gives a squeaky pop.
